text: The central theme of the volume is the sym- bolical representation of the psychic totality through the concept of the Self, whose tradi- tional historical equivalent is the figure of Christ.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Professor Jung demonstrates his thesis by an investigation of the A//egor/ae Christi, especially the fish symbol, but also of Gnostic and alchemical symbolism, which he treats as phenomena of cultural assimilation.

especially  the  fish  symbol,  but  also  of  Gnostic
and  alchemical  symbolism,  which  he  treats  as
phenomena  of  cultural  assimilation.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The theme of this work 1 is the idea of the Aeon (Greek, Aion).
text_raw: The  theme  of  this  work 1  is  the  idea  of  the  Aeon  (Greek,  Aion).

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: My investigation seeks, with the help of Christian, Gnostic, and alchemical symbols of the self, to throw light on the change of psychic situation within the "Christian aeon." Christian tradi- tion from the outset is not only saturated with Persian and Jewish ideas about the beginning and end of time, but is filled with intimations of a kind of enantiodromian reversal of domi- nants.
text_raw:
My  investigation  seeks,  with  the  help  of  Christian,  Gnostic,  and
alchemical  symbols  of  the  self,  to  throw  light  on  the  change  of
psychic  situation  within  the  "Christian  aeon."  Christian  tradi-
tion from  the  outset  is  not  only  saturated  with  Persian  and
Jewish  ideas  about  the  beginning  and  end  of  time,  but  is  filled
with  intimations  of  a  kind  of  enantiodromian  reversal  of  domi-
nants.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: I mean by this the dilemma of Christ and Antichrist.
text_raw: I  mean  by  this  the  dilemma  of  Christ  and  Antichrist.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Probably most of the historical speculations about time and the division of time were influenced, as the Apocalypse shows, by astrological ideas.
text_raw:
Probably  most  of  the  historical  speculations  about  time  and  the
division  of  time  were  influenced,  as  the  Apocalypse  shows,  by
astrological  ideas.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: It is therefore only natural that my reflections should gravitate mainly round the symbol of the Fishes, for the Pisces aeon is the synchronistic concomitant of two thousand years of Christian development.
text_raw:
It  is  therefore  only  natural  that  my  reflections
should  gravitate  mainly  round  the  symbol  of  the  Fishes,  for  the
Pisces  aeon  is  the  synchronistic  concomitant  of  two  thousand
years  of  Christian  development.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: In this time-period not only was the figure of the Anthropos (the "Son of Man") progres- sively amplified symbolically, and thus assimilated psychologi- cally, but it brought with it changes in man's attitude that had already been anticipated by the expectation of the Antichrist in the ancient texts.
text_raw:
In  this  time-period  not  only
was  the  figure  of  the  Anthropos  (the  "Son  of  Man")  progres-
sively amplified  symbolically,  and  thus  assimilated  psychologi-
cally, but  it  brought  with  it  changes  in  man's  attitude  that  had
already  been  anticipated  by  the  expectation  of  the  Antichrist
in  the  ancient  texts.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Because these texts relegate the appearance of Antichrist to the end of time, we are justified in speaking of a "Christian aeon," which, it was presupposed, would find its end with the Second Coming.
text_raw:
Because  these  texts  relegate  the  appearance
of  Antichrist  to  the  end  of  time,  we  are  justified  in  speaking  of
a  "Christian  aeon,"  which,  it  was  presupposed,  would  find  its
end  with  the  Second  Coming.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: It seems as if this expectation coincides with the astrological conception of the "Platonic month" of the Fishes.
text_raw:
It  seems  as  if  this  expectation
coincides  with  the  astrological  conception  of  the  "Platonic
month"  of  the  Fishes.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: "In this volume (VIII of the Psychologische Abhandlungen) I am bringing out two works which, despite their inner and outer differences, belong together in so far as they both treat of the great theme of this book, namely the idea of the Aeon (Greek, Aion).
text_raw:
"In  this  volume  (VIII  of
the  Psychologische  Abhandlungen)  I  am  bringing  out  two  works  which,  despite
their  inner  and  outer  differences,  belong  together  in  so  far  as  they  both  treat
of  the  great  theme  of  this  book,  namely  the  idea  of  the  Aeon  (Greek,  Aion).

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: While the contribution of my co-worker, Dr. Marie-Louise von Franz, describes the psychological transition from antiquity to Christianity by analysing the Pas- sion of St. Perpetua, my own investigation seeks, with the help of" etc., as above.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The immediate occasion for my proposing to discuss these historical questions is the fact that the archetypal image of wholeness, which appears so frequently in the products of the unconscious, has its forerunners in history.
text_raw:
The  immediate  occasion  for  my  proposing  to  discuss  these
historical  questions  is  the  fact  that  the  archetypal  image  of
wholeness,  which  appears  so  frequently  in  the  products  of  the
unconscious,  has  its  forerunners  in  history.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: These were identi- fied very early with the figure of Christ, as I have shown in my book Psychology and Alchemy.2 I have been requested so often by my readers to discuss the relations between the traditional Christ-figure and the natural symbols of wholeness, or the self, that I finally decided to take this task in hand.
text_raw:
These  were  identi-
fied very  early  with  the  figure  of  Christ,  as  I  have  shown  in  my
book  Psychology  and  Alchemy.2  I  have  been  requested  so  often
by  my  readers  to  discuss  the  relations  between  the  traditional
Christ-figure  and  the  natural  symbols  of  wholeness,  or  the
self,  that  I  finally  decided  to  take  this  task  in  hand.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Considering the unusual difficulties of such an undertaking, my decision did not come easily to me, for, in order to surmount all the ob- stacles and possibilities of error, a knowledge and caution would be needed which, unfortunately, are vouchsafed me only in limited degree.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: I am moderately certain of my observations on the empirical material, but I am fully aware of the risk I am taking in drawing the testimonies of history into the scope of my reflections.

the  empirical  material,  but  I  am  fully  aware  of  the  risk  I  am

chapter_title: Frontmatter

text_raw: THE  EGO

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Investigation of the psychology of the unconscious con- fronted me with facts which required the formulation of new concepts.
text_raw:
Investigation  of  the  psychology  of  the  unconscious  con-
fronted me  with  facts  which  required  the  formulation  of  new
concepts.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: One of these concepts is the self.
text_raw: One  of  these  concepts  is  the  self.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The entity so denoted is not meant to take the place of the one that has always been known as the ego, but includes it in a supraordinate concept.
text_raw:
The  entity  so  denoted
is  not  meant  to  take  the  place  of  the  one  that  has  always  been
known  as  the  ego,  but  includes  it  in  a  supraordinate  concept.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: We understand the ego as the complex factor to which all con- scious contents are related.
text_raw:
We  understand  the  ego  as  the  complex  factor  to  which  all  con-
scious contents  are  related.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: It forms, as it were, the centre of the field of consciousness; and, in so far as this comprises the em- pirical personality, the ego is the subject of all personal acts of consciousness.
text_raw:
It  forms,  as  it  were,  the  centre  of  the
field  of  consciousness;  and,  in  so  far  as  this  comprises  the  em-
pirical personality,  the  ego  is  the  subject  of  all  personal  acts  of
consciousness.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The relation of a psychic content to the ego forms the criterion of its consciousness, for no content can be con- scious unless it is represented to a subject.
text_raw:
The  relation  of  a  psychic  content  to  the  ego  forms
the  criterion  of  its  consciousness,  for  no  content  can  be  con-
scious unless  it  is  represented  to  a  subject.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: With this definition we have described and delimited the scope of the subject.
text_raw:
With  this  definition  we  have  described  and  delimited  the
scope  of  the  subject.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Theoretically, no limits can be set to the field of consciousness, since it is capable of indefinite extension.
text_raw:
Theoretically,  no  limits  can  be  set  to  the
field  of  consciousness,  since  it  is  capable  of  indefinite  extension.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Empirically, however, it always finds its limit when it comes up against the unknown.
text_raw:
Empirically,  however,  it  always  finds  its  limit  when  it  comes  up
against  the  unknown.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: This consists of everything we do not know, which, therefore, is not related to the ego as the centre of the field of consciousness.
text_raw:
This  consists  of  everything  we  do  not
know,  which,  therefore,  is  not  related  to  the  ego  as  the  centre
of  the  field  of  consciousness.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The unknown falls into two groups of objects: those which are outside and can be experienced by the senses, and those which are inside and are experienced im- mediately.
text_raw:
The  unknown  falls  into  two  groups
of  objects:  those  which  are  outside  and  can  be  experienced  by
the  senses,  and  those  which  are  inside  and  are  experienced  im-
mediately.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The first group comprises the unknown in the outer world; the second the unknown in the inner world.
text_raw:
The  first  group  comprises  the  unknown  in  the  outer
world;  the  second  the  unknown  in  the  inner  world.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: We call this latter territory the unconscious.
text_raw:
We  call  this
latter  territory  the  unconscious.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The ego, as a specific content of consciousness, is not a sim- ple or elementary factor but a complex one which, as such, cannot be described exhaustively.
text_raw:
The  ego,  as  a  specific  content  of  consciousness,  is  not  a  sim-
ple or  elementary  factor  but  a  complex  one  which,  as  such,
cannot  be  described  exhaustively.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Experience shows that it rests on two seemingly different bases: the somatic and the psychic.
text_raw:
Experience  shows  that  it  rests
on  two  seemingly  different  bases:  the  somatic  and  the  psychic.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The somatic basis is inferred from the totality of endosomatic perceptions, which for their part are already of a psychic nature and are associated with the ego, and are therefore conscious.
text_raw:
The  somatic  basis  is  inferred  from  the  totality  of  endosomatic
perceptions,  which  for  their  part  are  already  of  a  psychic  nature
and  are  associated  with  the  ego,  and  are  therefore  conscious.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: They are produced by endosomatic stimuli, only some of which
text_raw: They  are  produced  by  endosomatic  stimuli,  only  some  of  which

chapter_title: Frontmatter
Frontmatter
text: AION
text_raw: AION

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: cross the threshold of consciousness.
text_raw: cross  the  threshold  of  consciousness.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: A considerable proportion of these stimuli occur unconsciously, that is, subliminally.
text_raw:
A  considerable  proportion
of  these  stimuli  occur  unconsciously,  that  is,  subliminally.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The fact that they are subliminal does not necessarily mean that their status is merely physiological, any more than this would be true of a psychic content.
text_raw:
The
fact  that  they  are  subliminal  does  not  necessarily  mean  that  their
status  is  merely  physiological,  any  more  than  this  would  be  true
of  a  psychic  content.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Sometimes they are capable of crossing the threshold, that is, of becoming perceptions.
text_raw:
Sometimes  they  are  capable  of  crossing  the
threshold,  that  is,  of  becoming  perceptions.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: But there is no doubt that a large proportion of these endosomatic stimuli are simply incapable of consciousness and are so elementary that there is no reason to assign them a psychic natureâ€” unless of course one favours the philosophical view that all life-processes are psychic anyway.
text_raw:
But  there  is  no
doubt  that  a  large  proportion  of  these  endosomatic  stimuli  are
simply  incapable  of  consciousness  and  are  so  elementary  that
there  is  no  reason  to  assign  them  a  psychic  natureâ€” unless  of
course  one  favours  the  philosophical  view  that  all  life-processes
are  psychic  anyway.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The chief objection to this hardly demon- strable hypothesis is that it enlarges the concept of the psyche beyond all bounds and interprets the life-process in a way not absolutely warranted by the facts.
text_raw:
The  chief  objection  to  this  hardly  demon-
strable hypothesis  is  that  it  enlarges  the  concept  of  the  psyche
beyond  all  bounds  and  interprets  the  life-process  in  a  way  not
absolutely  warranted  by  the  facts.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Concepts that are too broad usually prove to be unsuitable instruments because they are too vague and nebulous.
text_raw:
Concepts  that  are  too  broad
usually  prove  to  be  unsuitable  instruments  because  they  are  too
vague  and  nebulous.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: I have therefore suggested that the term "psychic" be used only where there is evidence of a will capable of modifying reflex or instinctual processes.
text_raw:
I  have  therefore  suggested  that  the  term
"psychic"  be  used  only  where  there  is  evidence  of  a  will  capable
of  modifying  reflex  or  instinctual  processes.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Here I must refer the reader to my paper "On the Nature of the Psyche," * where I have discussed this definition of the "psychic" at somewhat greater length.
text_raw:
Here  I  must  refer
the  reader  to  my  paper  "On  the  Nature  of  the  Psyche,"  *  where
I  have  discussed  this  definition  of  the  "psychic"  at  somewhat
greater  length.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The somatic basis of the ego consists, then, of conscious and unconscious factors.
text_raw:
The  somatic  basis  of  the  ego  consists,  then,  of  conscious  and
unconscious  factors.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The same is true of the psychic basis: on the one hand the ego rests on the total field of consciousness, and on the other, on the sum total of unconscious contents.
text_raw:
The  same  is  true  of  the  psychic  basis:  on
the  one  hand  the  ego  rests  on  the  total  field  of  consciousness,
and  on  the  other,  on  the  sum  total  of  unconscious  contents.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: These fall into three groups: first, temporarily subliminal con- tents that can be reproduced voluntarily (memory); second, unconscious contents that cannot be reproduced voluntarily; third, contents that are not capable of becoming conscious at all.
text_raw:
These  fall  into  three  groups:  first,  temporarily  subliminal  con-
tents that  can  be  reproduced  voluntarily  (memory);  second,
unconscious  contents  that  cannot  be  reproduced  voluntarily;
third,  contents  that  are  not  capable  of  becoming  conscious  at  all.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Group two can be inferred from the spontaneous irruption of subliminal contents into consciousness.
text_raw:
Group  two  can  be  inferred  from  the  spontaneous  irruption  of
subliminal  contents  into  consciousness.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Group three is hypo- thetical; it is a logical inference from the facts underlying group two.
text_raw:
Group  three  is  hypo-
thetical; it  is  a  logical  inference  from  the  facts  underlying  group
two.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: It contains contents which have not yet irrupted into con- sciousness, or which never will.
text_raw:
It  contains  contents  which  have  not  yet  irrupted  into  con-
sciousness, or  which  never  will.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: When I said that the ego "rests" on the total field of con- sciousness I do not mean that it consists of this.
text_raw:
When  I  said  that  the  ego  "rests"  on  the  total  field  of  con-
sciousness I  do  not  mean  that  it  consists  of  this.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Were that so, it would be indistinguishable from the field of consciousness as a whole.
text_raw:
Were  that  so,  it
would  be  indistinguishable  from  the  field  of  consciousness  as  a
whole.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The ego is only the latter's point of reference, grounded on and limited by the somatic factor described above, l Pars.
text_raw:
The  ego  is  only  the  latter's  point  of  reference,  grounded
on  and  limited  by  the  somatic  factor  described  above,
l  Pars.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
Frontmatter
text: THE EGO
text_raw: THE   EGO

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Although its bases are in themselves relatively unknown and unconscious, the ego is a conscious factor par excellence.
text_raw:
Although  its  bases  are  in  themselves  relatively  unknown  and
unconscious,  the  ego  is  a  conscious  factor  par  excellence.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: It is even acquired, empirically speaking, during the individual's lifetime.
text_raw:
It  is
even  acquired,  empirically  speaking,  during  the  individual's
lifetime.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: It seems to arise in the first place from the collision between the somatic factor and the environment, and, once established as a subject, it goes on developing from further col- lisions with the outer world and the inner.
text_raw:
It  seems  to  arise  in  the  first  place  from  the  collision
between  the  somatic  factor  and  the  environment,  and,  once
established  as  a  subject,  it  goes  on  developing  from  further  col-
lisions with  the  outer  world  and  the  inner.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Despite the unlimited extent of its bases, the ego is never more and never less than consciousness as a whole.
text_raw:
Despite  the  unlimited  extent  of  its  bases,  the  ego  is  never
more  and  never  less  than  consciousness  as  a  whole.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: As a con- scious factor the ego could, theoretically at least, be described completely.
text_raw:
As  a  con-
scious factor  the  ego  could,  theoretically  at  least,  be  described
completely.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: But this would never amount to more than a pic- ture of the conscious personality; all those features which are unknown or unconscious to the subject would be missing.
text_raw:
But  this  would  never  amount  to  more  than  a  pic-
ture of  the  conscious  personality;  all  those  features  which  are
unknown  or  unconscious  to  the  subject  would  be  missing.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: A total picture would have to include these.
text_raw:
A
total  picture  would  have  to  include  these.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: But a total descrip- tion of the personality is, even in theory, absolutely impossible, because the unconscious portion of it cannot be grasped cogni- tively.
text_raw:
But  a  total  descrip-
tion of  the  personality  is,  even  in  theory,  absolutely  impossible,
because  the  unconscious  portion  of  it  cannot  be  grasped  cogni-
tively.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: This unconscious portion, as experience has abundantly shown, is by no means unimportant.
text_raw:
This  unconscious  portion,  as  experience  has  abundantly
shown,  is  by  no  means  unimportant.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: On the contrary, the most decisive qualities in a person are often unconscious and can be perceived only by others, or have to be laboriously discovered with outside help.
text_raw:
On  the  contrary,  the  most
decisive  qualities  in  a  person  are  often  unconscious  and  can  be
perceived  only  by  others,  or  have  to  be  laboriously  discovered
with  outside  help.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Clearly, then, the personality as a total phenomenon does not coincide with the ego, that is, with the conscious personality, but forms an entity that has to be distinguished from the ego.
text_raw:
Clearly,  then,  the  personality  as  a  total  phenomenon  does
not  coincide  with  the  ego,  that  is,  with  the  conscious  personality,
but  forms  an  entity  that  has  to  be  distinguished  from  the  ego.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Naturally the need to do this is incumbent only on a psychology that reckons with the fact of the unconscious, but for such a psychology the distinction is of paramount importance.
text_raw:
Naturally  the  need  to  do  this  is  incumbent  only  on  a  psychology
that  reckons  with  the  fact  of  the  unconscious,  but  for  such  a
psychology  the  distinction  is  of  paramount  importance.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Even for jurisprudence it should be of some importance whether certain psychic facts are conscious or not â€” for instance, in adjudging the question of responsibility.
text_raw:
Even  for
jurisprudence  it  should  be  of  some  importance  whether  certain
psychic  facts  are  conscious  or  not â€” for  instance,  in  adjudging  the
question  of  responsibility.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: I have suggested calling the total personality which, though present, cannot be fully known, the self.
text_raw:
I  have  suggested  calling  the  total  personality  which,  though
present,  cannot  be  fully  known,  the  self.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The ego is, by defini- tion, subordinate to the self and is related to it like a part to the whole.
text_raw:
The  ego  is,  by  defini-
tion, subordinate  to  the  self  and  is  related  to  it  like  a  part  to  the
whole.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Inside the field of consciousness it has, as we say, free will.
text_raw:
Inside  the  field  of  consciousness  it  has,  as  we  say,  free
will.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: By this I do not mean anything philosophical, only the well-known psychological fact of "free choice," or rather the sub- jective feeling of freedom.
text_raw:
By  this  I  do  not  mean  anything  philosophical,  only  the
well-known  psychological  fact  of  "free  choice,"  or  rather  the  sub-
jective feeling  of  freedom.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: But, just as our free will clashes with necessity in the outside world, so also it finds its limits outside the field of consciousness in the subjective inner world, where it comes into conflict with the facts of the self.
text_raw:
But,  just  as  our  free  will  clashes  with
necessity  in  the  outside  world,  so  also  it  finds  its  limits  outside
the  field  of  consciousness  in  the  subjective  inner  world,  where
it  comes  into  conflict  with  the  facts  of  the  self.

text: And just as

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: If we discount certain suggestive ideas in Leibniz, Kant, Schelling, and Schopenhauer, and the philosophical excursions of Carus and von Hartmann, it is only since the end of the nineteenth century that modern psychology, with its inductive methods, has discovered the foundations of consciousness and proved empirically the exist- ence of a psyche outside consciousness.

is  only  since  the  end  of  the  nineteenth  century  that  modern
psychology,  with  its  inductive  methods,  has  discovered  the
foundations  of  consciousness  and  proved  empirically  the  exist-
ence of  a  psyche  outside  consciousness.

text: But from the standpoint of the psychology of the personality a twofold division ensues: an "extra-conscious" psyche whose contents are personal, and an "extra-conscious" psyche whose contents are impersonal and collective.

text: The image of wholeness then remains in the unconscious, so that on the one hand it shares the archaic nature of the unconscious and on the other finds itself in the psychically relative space-time continuum that is characteristic of the unconscious as such.4 Both these qualities are numinous and hence have an unlimited determining effect on ego-con- sciousness, which is differentiated, i.e., separated, from the un- conscious and moreover exists in an absolute space and an absolute time.

text: This way of looking at it can, with some show of justice, be accused not only of being very convenient but of cloaking moral laxity in the mantle of virtue.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The feeling-value is a very important criterion which psychology cannot do without, because it determines in large measure the role which the content will play in the psychic economy.

The  feeling-value  is  a  very  important  criterion  which
psychology  cannot  do  without,  because  it  determines  in  large
measure  the  role  which  the  content  will  play  in  the  psychic
economy.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: That is to say, the affective value gives the measure of the intensity of an idea, and the intensity in its turn expresses that idea's energic tension, its effective potential.
text_raw:
That  is  to  say,  the  affective  value  gives  the  measure  of
the  intensity  of  an  idea,  and  the  intensity  in  its  turn  expresses
that  idea's  energic  tension,  its  effective  potential.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The shadow, for instance, usually has a decidedly negative feeling- value, while the anima, like the animus, has more of a positive one.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Whereas the shadow is accompanied by more or less definite and describable feeling-tones, the anima and animus exhibit feeling qualities that are harder to define.

and  describable  feeling-tones,  the  anima  and  animus  exhibit
feeling  qualities  that  are  harder  to  define.

text: Since psychology is not metaphysics, no metaphysical dualism can be derived from, or imputed to, its statements concerning the equivalence of opposites.74 It knows that equivalent oppo- sites are necessary conditions inherent in the act of cognition, and that without them no discrimination would be possible.
text_raw:
Since  psychology  is  not  metaphysics,  no  metaphysical  dualism
can  be  derived  from,  or  imputed  to,  its  statements  concerning
the  equivalence  of  opposites.74  It  knows  that  equivalent  oppo-
sites  are  necessary  conditions  inherent  in  the  act  of  cognition,
and  that  without  them  no  discrimination  would  be  possible.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: This characteristic coincides with the claim of Christianity to be the beginning and end of all things, and with its eschato- logical expectation of the end of the world and the coming of God's kingdom.49 Thus the astrological characteristics of the fish contain essential components of the Christian myth; first, the cross; second, the moral conflict and its splitting into the figures of Christ and Antichrist; third, the motif of the son of a virgin; fourth, the classical mother-son tragedy; fifth, the danger at birth; and sixth, the saviour and bringer of healing.

This  characteristic  coincides  with  the  claim  of  Christianity  to
be  the  beginning  and  end  of  all  things,  and  with  its  eschato-
logical  expectation  of  the  end  of  the  world  and  the  coming  of
God's  kingdom.49  Thus  the  astrological  characteristics  of  the
fish  contain  essential  components  of  the  Christian  myth;  first,
the  cross;  second,  the  moral  conflict  and  its  splitting  into  the
figures  of  Christ  and  Antichrist;  third,  the  motif  of  the  son  of  a
virgin;  fourth,  the  classical  mother-son  tragedy;  fifth,  the  danger
at  birth;  and  sixth,  the  saviour  and  bringer  of  healing.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: At about the same time, or a little later, its appendices were also translated, namely the "Allegoriae super librum Turbae," the "Allegoriae sapientum supra librum Turbae XXIX distinctiones," 1 together with the "Aenigmata ex Visione Arislei" and "In Turbam philoso- phorum exercitationes." The Turba belongs to the same sphere of thought as the Tabula smaragdina, and hence is one of those late Hellenistic products that were transmitted to us by the Arabs, mainly, perhaps, through the Neoplatonic school of Harran (Thabit ibn Qurrah and others), which flourished at the beginning of the eleventh century.2 The ideas preserved in these treatises are 'Alexandrian," and the recipes, particularly those set forth in the "Allegoriae super librum Turbae," adhere closely to the spirit and letter of the Papyri Graecae Magicae.3

text: 203 According to Blaise de Vigenere, the fire has not two but four aspects: the intelligible, which is all light; the heavenly, partaking of heat and light; the elemental, pertaining to the lower world and compounded of light, heat, and glow (ardor); and finally the infernal, opposed to the intelligible, glowing and burning without any light.33 Here again we encounter the quaternity which the ancients associated with fire, as we saw from the Egyptian conception of Set and the four sons of Horus,34 and from Ezekiel's vision of the fiery region to the north.
text_raw:
203  According  to  Blaise  de  Vigenere,  the  fire  has  not  two  but
four  aspects:  the  intelligible,  which  is  all  light;  the  heavenly,
partaking  of  heat  and  light;  the  elemental,  pertaining  to  the
lower  world  and  compounded  of  light,  heat,  and  glow  (ardor);
and  finally  the  infernal,  opposed  to  the  intelligible,  glowing
and  burning  without  any  light.33  Here  again  we  encounter  the
quaternity  which  the  ancients  associated  with  fire,  as  we  saw
from  the  Egyptian  conception  of  Set  and  the  four  sons  of
Horus,34  and  from  Ezekiel's  vision  of  the  fiery  region  to  the
north.

text: This little fish is extremely small, alone, and unique in its shape, but the sea is great and vast, and hence it is impossible for those to catch it who do not know in what part of the world it dwells.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Believe me verily, that he who, as Theophrastus says, does not well understand the art by which he can draw down the moon from the sky and bring it from heaven to earth, and change it into water and then into earth, will never find the material of the stone of the wise, for it is not more difficult to perform the one than to find the other.
text_raw:

change  it  into  water  and  then  into  earth,  will  never  find  the  material
of  the  stone  of  the  wise,  for  it  is  not  more  difficult  to  perform  the  one
than  to  find  the  other.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Yet none the less, when we speak somewhat in confidence in the ear of a trusted friend, we teach him that hidden secret of the wise, how he can naturally, speedily, and easily catch the little fish called Remora, which is able to hold back the proud vessels of the great Ocean sea (that is the spirit of the world).

proud  vessels  of  the  great  Ocean  sea  (that  is  the  spirit  of  the  world).

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: For an alchemist living' in the early part of the seventeenth century, the "spirit of the world" is a somewhat unusual term, because the expression more commonly used was the "anima mundi." The world-soul or, in this case, the world-spirit is a projection of the unconscious, there being no method or appara- tus which could provide an objective experience of this kind and thus furnish objective proof of the world's animation.

text: In the present instance the fishes would characterize the ascendent, the moment of the world's birth.96 Now we know that cosmogonic myths are, at bottom, symbols for the coming of consciousness (though I cannot go into this here).97 The dawn-state corresponds to the unconscious; in alchemical terms, it is the chaos, the massa confusa or nigredo; and by means of the opus, which the adept likens to the creation of the world, the albedo or dealbatio is produced, the whitening, which is com- pared sometimes to the full moon, sometimes to sunrise.98 It also means illumination, the broadening of consciousness that goes hand in hand with the "work." Expressed psychologically, therefore, the two fishes which the devil found on the primeval waters would signify the newly arisen world of consciousness.

text: The attraction, so the historical tradition says, emanates from the fish and brings the vessel, whether powered by sail or oarsmen, to a standstill.1 I mention this seemingly unimportant feature because, as we shall see, in the alchemical view the attraction no longer proceeds from the fish but from a magnet which man possesses and which exerts the attraction that was once the mysterious property of the fish.

text: But a psychic function was absolutely necessary to it when, as in the case of the magnesia, the adept was preoccupied with one of the innumerable expres- sions used for the unconscious, that is, for the hidden part of the psyche that had slipped into the unknown chemical com- pound by projection, and that bedevilled and befooled him in the guise of a hundred "arcane substances." text: 246 Obviously a distinction must be made between two cate- gories of symbols: first, those which refer to the extrapsychic chemical substance or its metaphysical equivalent, e.g., serpens mercurialis, spiritus, anima mundi, Veritas, sapientia, etc.; sec- ond, those denoting the chemical preparations produced by the adept, such as solvents (aqua, acetum, lac virginis) or their "phil- osophical" equivalent, the theoria or scientia, which, when it is "right," has miraculous effects on matter, as Dorn explains in his philosophical treatises.32
